They treat the activity as a one-time gate rather than an ongoing practice. They involve only security specialists, missing the knowledge of those who understand the system best. They generate long lists of threats but do not assign owners or track mitigations. And they ignore threats from trusted insiders and from third-party components and dependencies, which are significant sources of real-world incidents.

Complementary Methods

STRIDE is only one approach. Attack trees describe how an attacker might achieve a goal through branches of alternative steps. PASTA is a risk-centric methodology that connects technical threats to business impact. The MITRE ATT&CK knowledge base catalogs real adversary behavior and is useful for validating that detection and response cover techniques seen in the wild. LINDDUN extends the thinking to privacy threats. Teams can combine these methods according to their needs.

Key Takeaways

Threat modeling turns security from an afterthought into a design activity. Draw the system, identify trust boundaries, apply STRIDE to each element, choose and prioritize mitigations, and keep the model up to date. Even an informal session with a whiteboard and the right people can reveal important weaknesses early and build a lasting culture of security awareness.

title: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) Overview
content:
What It Is

Cross-site scripting is a vulnerability in which an application includes untrusted data in a web page without proper handling, allowing an attacker's script to run in the browser of another user. The script executes with the privileges of the vulnerable site, so it can read page content, act on behalf of the user and interact with the application as if the user had done so.

Types

Reflected XSS occurs when input from a request is immediately included in the response. Stored XSS occurs when malicious input is saved, for example in a comment, and shown to later visitors. DOM-based XSS occurs entirely in client-side code that writes untrusted data into the page in an unsafe way.

Prevention

Encode output according to the context in which it appears, such as HTML body, attribute, JavaScript or URL. Prefer frameworks that escape by default and avoid unsafe sinks such as direct HTML insertion. Sanitize rich content with a well-maintained library. Add a Content Security Policy to limit which scripts can execute, set cookies with the HttpOnly and SameSite attributes, and validate input as an additional layer.

Testing

Include XSS checks in code review, static analysis and dynamic scanning, and test every place where user-controlled data is displayed.

title: Zero Trust Architecture in Brief
content:
Concept

Zero trust is a security model built on the principle of never trust, always verify. Traditional designs treated the internal network as a trusted zone and the internet as hostile, so anything that got inside could move freely. Remote work, cloud services and mobile devices have dissolved that boundary. Zero trust assumes that an attacker may already be present and requires every request to be authenticated, authorized and evaluated in context.

Core Principles

Verify explicitly by using identity, device health, location and behavior for each access decision. Use least privilege so that users and workloads receive only the access they need, for only as long as they need it. Assume breach by segmenting resources, encrypting traffic and monitoring continuously to detect and contain intrusions.

Typical Building Blocks

A strong identity provider with multi-factor authentication, a device management and compliance system, policy engines that make access decisions, micro-segmentation to restrict lateral movement, and centralized logging and analytics.

Getting Started

Begin with an inventory of users, devices, applications and data. Protect the most valuable assets first, move one application at a time behind identity-aware access, and measure improvements. Zero trust is a journey rather than a single product.
